standard.title: Compare features of target language and English texts
standard.description: recognise and compare features of familiar spoken and written text in the target language and English
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare structural features, vocabulary and text features across the target language and English using simple metalanguage (AC9LCH2U03). They have used metalanguage for basic word types. They have not yet compared texts systematically by genre or feature type, used metalanguage to describe grammar rules, or analysed how English influences everyday target language use.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and compare features of familiar spoken and written texts in the target language and English — including genre features, grammatical conventions, layout, and cross-linguistic influence — using metalanguage.

nodes.label: Genre features and text purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify features of different text genres in the target language and English, and discuss what makes each genre appropriate for its purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different text genres in the target language (e.g. narrative, procedural, informative) and describe at least two features that distinguish each genre.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise features of narratives, procedural and explanatory texts; identify language features and symbols associated with different text types; compare the features of the same genre across target language and English texts; discuss which genres suit different purposes and audiences.
wider: Compare the same genre text in target language and English — identify all the structural and language feature differences and discuss what they reveal about how the genre convention differs across the two languages
Create a short genre comparison guide for a peer — explaining how to recognise a particular genre in both languages and what conventions must be followed
nodes.hinge_reason: Genre feature knowledge is the prerequisite for all text comparison work. Students who cannot identify genre-level features cannot compare texts systematically — they can only notice surface differences. Genre awareness also underpins all text creation in the creating strand.

response_modes.reason: Genre analysis requires students to apply a framework — what are the features of this genre? — to both familiar and new texts. Explicit genre study with named features (orientation, complication, resolution; materials, steps, result) builds the analytical vocabulary before students can compare independently.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two text genres in the target language with at least two distinguishing features each
Can explain which genre would be most appropriate for a given purpose and why

nodes.label: Metalanguage for grammar comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use metalanguage to describe grammar rules in the target language and compare grammatical conventions across the target language and English.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least four metalanguage terms correctly in describing a grammar rule or comparison between the target language and English.
nodes.typical_width: Use metalanguage to describe placement rules, word class functions and sentence-level patterns in the target language; compare grammatical conventions with English; identify where similar terms describe different grammatical functions across the two languages.
wider: Annotate a short target language text using metalanguage labels — then compare the annotation with an equivalent English text annotation and identify structural differences
Investigate a grammatical feature that is named differently or functions differently in the target language metalanguage versus English metalanguage — explain the difference to a peer

response_modes.reason: Metalanguage for grammar is built through repeated use across different comparison tasks — not through a single lesson on terminology. Students need to encounter and deploy metalanguage across multiple text analysis and comparison contexts before it becomes functional vocabulary.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners who already use grammar intuitively gain significant analytical leverage from metalanguage — it allows them to describe and explain what they already do, not just follow rules. Width investment here builds the explanatory capacity that is valuable for academic language learning across both languages.
success_criteria: Uses at least four metalanguage terms correctly in a grammar description or comparison
Explains at least one grammatical rule in the target language using metalanguage

nodes.label: Cross-linguistic influence and text features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify examples of cross-linguistic influence in everyday target language use and compare layout, script and textual features across target language and English texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of English influence on everyday target language use and at least two textual feature differences between a target language and English text.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how English influences informal everyday target language use — borrowed words, code-switching, adapted expressions; compare layout, heading, script and organisational features of target language and English texts; identify similarities and differences in how the same information is organised across text types.
wider: Research the history of a specific borrowed word or expression — trace where it came from and how it entered everyday target language use
Create a bilingual comparison display showing how the same text type is structured differently in target language and English — annotate the key differences

response_modes.reason: Cross-linguistic influence and textual feature comparison integrates genre awareness (node 1) and grammar metalanguage (node 2) into a full text-level analysis. The teaching investment is in making visible what students often see as normal — the way English has entered everyday target language, and the distinct textual conventions of each language.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two examples of English influence on everyday target language use
Identifies at least two textual feature differences between a target language and English text of the same type
